claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The Chd1 protein has a C-terminal DNA-binding domain (DBD) that is made up of SANT and SLIDE domains.
claims.source: The Chd1 protein has a C-terminal DNA-binding domain (DBD) that is made up of SANT and SLIDE domains that are also present in ISWI proteins (Grüne et al., 2003; Ryan et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The C-terminal DNA-binding domain is required for efficient nucleosome repositioning in Chd1.
claims.source: This second DNA-binding interface is required for efficient nucleosome repositioning both in the context of Chd1 (Patel et al., 2013; Ryan et al., 2011; Sharma et al., 2011) and ISWI proteins (Dang and Bartholomew, 2007; Grüne et al., 2003; Hota et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Substitution of the Chd1 DBD with a heterologous DBD directs nucleosome positioning towards the DNA bound by this domain.
claims.source: Remarkably, substitution of this domain with a heterologous DBD directs nucleosome positioning towards the DNA bound by this domain (McKnight et al., 2011; Patel et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The ATPase domain of ISW2 engages with nucleosomal DNA near super helical location (SHL) 2, two turns from the dyad axis of symmetry.
claims.source: Application of this approach to study the ISW2 enzyme showed that the ATPase domain engages with nucleosomal DNA near super helical location (SHL) 2, two turns from the dyad axis of symmetry.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from directed crosslinking studies.

claims.claim: In ISW2, the DNA-binding accessory subunits engage linker DNA extending up to 50 bp from the edge of the nucleosome.
claims.source: In the case of ISW2, the DNA-binding accessory subunits are observed to engage linker DNA extending up to 50 bp from the edge of the nucleosome (Dang and Bartholomew, 2007; Kagalwala et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Two ISWI complexes can engage a single nucleosome.
claims.source: In the case of ISWI containing enzymes, it has been shown that two complexes can engage a single nucleosome (Racki et al., 2009) and this can facilitate the bidirectional movement of nucleosomes (Blosser et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: DNA is removed from nucleosomes in kinetically coupled bursts of 3 bp that comprise of shorter single base increments during repositioning.
claims.source: These studies show that DNA is removed from nucleosomes in kinetically coupled bursts of 3 bp that comprise of shorter single base increments (Deindl et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: A series of fragments of Chd1 were expressed and purified for SAXS analysis.
claims.source: To help characterise the structure of intact Chd1, a series of fragments of Chd1 were expressed and purified (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claims.claim: SAXS data were collected for each Chd1 fragment.
claims.source: We then collected small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) data for each of these (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claims.claim: The hydrodynamic radius and molecular weight values obtained from SAXS are consistent with Chd1 being predominantly monomeric in solution.
claims.source: For each fragment, the hydrodynamic radius of the protein fragment and molecular weight in solution was calculated (Figure 1B). The values obtained are consistent with Chd1 being predominantly monomeric in solution.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of SAXS data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Volumes consistent with each scattering curve were calculated ab initio for Chd1 fragments.
claims.source: Volumes consistent with each scattering curve were calculated ab initio (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This describes the computational analysis of SAXS data.

claims.claim: The DBD can be docked within the volume obtained for the DBD fragment of Chd1.
claims.source: For example, the DBD can be docked within the volume obtained for this fragment of the protein and the chromoATPase domains within the volumes obtained for fragments that include this region.
claims.evidence: This describes the fitting of known structures into SAXS volumes.

claims.claim: The chromoATPase domains can be docked within the volumes obtained for fragments that include this region.
claims.source: For example, the DBD can be docked within the volume obtained for this fragment of the protein and the chromoATPase domains within the volumes obtained for fragments that include this region.
claims.evidence: This describes the fitting of known structures into SAXS volumes.

claims.claim: The DBD and N-terminal 133 residues contribute to the protrusion adjacent to one of the ATPase domains in the SAXS volume.
claims.source: This indicates that the DBD and N-terminal 133 residues contribute to the protrusion adjacent to one of the ATPase domains (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of SAXS data.

claims.claim: A cys-free mutant of Chd1 displays nucleosome remodelling activity comparable to the wild-type protein.
claims.source: Importantly, this cys-free mutant protein displays nucleosome remodelling activity comparable to the wild-type protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by activity assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Pairs of cysteine residues were introduced at specific sites in Chd1 1–1305 for PELDOR measurements.
claims.source: Pairs of cysteine residues were then introduced at specific sites in Chd1 1–1305 via site-directed mutagenesis and these sites were then labelled with the thiol-reactive reporter (1-Oxyl-2,2,5,5-tetramethylpyrroline-3-methyl) methanethiosulfonate (MTSL).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental approach for PELDOR measurements.

claims.claim: The experimentally measured distances from PELDOR correlate with the predicted distances derived from the chromoATPase crystal structure to within a few angstroms.
claims.source: The experimentally measured distances correlate with the predicted distances derived from the chromoATPase crystal structure (3MWY) (Hauk et al., 2010) to within a few angstroms (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of experimental PELDOR data with predictions from a crystal structure.

claims.claim: The structure of the chromoATPase domains is similar in solution to that observed in the crystal structure.
claims.source: This suggests that the structure of the chromoATPase domains is similar in solution to that observed in the crystal structure.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the agreement between PELDOR measurements and crystal structure predictions.

claims.claim: A total of 16 distinct distance measurements were made between different pairwise combinations of sites in the DBD and chromoATPase domains.
claims.source: A total of 16 distinct distance measurements were made between different pairwise combinations of these sites.
claims.evidence: This describes the extent of PELDOR measurements performed.

claims.claim: Measurements between locations within the DBD and ATPase lobe 1 gave rise to several well defined measurements.
claims.source: Measurements between locations within the DBD and ATPase lobe 1 gave rise to several well defined measurements where an oscillation is evident in the background corrected signal and a single major distance distribution can be extracted (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This describes the quality of PELDOR data for specific domain pairs.

claims.claim: Measurements between ATPase lobe 2 and the DBD were less well defined, often giving rise to multiple distance distributions.
claims.source: However, measurements between ATPase lobe 2 and the DBD were in general less well defined, often giving rise to multiple distance distributions with similar probabilities (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This describes the quality of PELDOR data for specific domain pairs.

claims.claim: The less well defined measurements between ATPase lobe 2 and the DBD likely arise from increased dynamics between these domains.
claims.source: This is likely to arise from increased dynamics between these domains.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the PELDOR data quality.

claims.claim: Measurements between chromodomains and the DBD did not provide tight single distance distributions.
claims.source: Similarly, measurements between chromodomains and the DBD did not provide tight single distance distributions (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This describes the quality of PELDOR data for specific domain pairs.

claims.claim: Two separate modelling approaches were used to determine the orientation of the DBD relative to the chromoATPase domains using PELDOR distance constraints.
claims.source: The most prominent distribution of distances for each pair of labelling sites (Shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 3–5) was used as a constraint in two separate modelling approaches.
claims.evidence: This describes the computational modeling approach.

claims.claim: Xplor-NIH was used for conjugated gradient minimisation with PELDOR distance constraints.
claims.source: In the first approach, a conjugated gradient minimisation was carried with centres of the modelled distribution of the nitroxide atoms NOE constraints in Xplor-NIH (Schwieters et al., 2003) (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This describes one computational modeling approach used.

claims.claim: TagDock was used to compute geometrically possible docking poses between the domains and evaluate those compatible with experimental distance constraints.
claims.source: In the second, TagDock (Smith et al., 2013) was used to compute all geometrically possible docking poses between the domains and evaluated those compatible with experimental distance constraints.
claims.evidence: This describes the second computational modeling approach used.

claims.claim: The Xplor approach yielded an ensemble of solutions with RMSD 2.8 Å.
claims.source: In both Xplor and TagDock approaches, an ensemble of solutions with RMSD 2.8 and 1.6 Å, respectively, were obtained.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the computational modeling.

claims.claim: The TagDock approach yielded an ensemble of solutions with RMSD 1.6 Å.
claims.source: In both Xplor and TagDock approaches, an ensemble of solutions with RMSD 2.8 and 1.6 Å, respectively, were obtained.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the computational modeling.

claims.claim: The average of the ensemble solutions obtained using the two approaches has an RMS deviation of 2.4 Å.
claims.source: In addition, the average of the ensemble solutions obtained using the two approaches has an RMS deviation of 2.4 Å.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of the two modeling approaches.

claims.claim: The PELDOR-derived model is compatible with the volume envelopes obtained from the SAXS data.
claims.source: The PELDOR-derived model is compatible with the volume envelopes obtained from the SAXS data (Figure 2—figure supplement 7A).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of PELDOR and SAXS data.

claims.claim: The SAXS pattern computed from the atomistic EPR-based model of Chd1 yields a poor fit to the experimental scattering data from the full length protein with discrepancy χ2= 11.5.
claims.source: The SAXS pattern computed by program CRYSOL (Svergun et al., 1995) from the atomistic EPR-based model of Chd1 yields a poor fit to the experimental scattering data from the full length protein with discrepancy χ2= 11.5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 7B).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of model and experimental data.

claims.claim: Significant parts of the Chd1 polypeptide are missing in the EPR-based model, which explains the poor fit to SAXS data.
claims.source: However, this misfit is to be expected given that significant parts of the polypeptide (174 and 36 residues at the N- and C-termini, respectively, and a 82-residue linker between chromoATPase and DBD domains) are missing in the Chd1 model.
claims.evidence: This is an explanation for the discrepancy between model and data.

claims.claim: The program BUNCH was used to reconstruct probable configurations of missing portions of Chd1 as dummy residue chains.
claims.source: To address this, the program BUNCH was used to reconstruct probable configurations of these missing portions in the form of dummy residue (DR) chains (Petoukhov and Svergun, 2005).
claims.evidence: This describes a computational approach to improve the model.

claims.claim: The addition of the missing loops significantly improved the agreement between the experimental and the calculated SAXS data with χ2 improving from 11.5 to 2.08.
claims.source: The addition of the missing loops significantly improved the agreement between the experimental and the calculated data with χ2 improving from 11.5 to 2.08 (Figure 2—figure supplement 7B).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result showing improved model fit.

claims.claim: Chemical crosslinking coupled with mass spectrometry using BS3 identified several crosslinks between the N-terminal region of Chd1 and the DBD.
claims.source: Interestingly, several crosslinks between the N-terminal region of Chd1 and the DBD are also identified (Figure 3A), suggesting these two regions are close to one another in the intact protein.
claims.evidence: This is a result from crosslinking mass spectrometry experiments.

claims.claim: The N-terminal region of Chd1 and the DBD are close to one another in the intact protein.
claims.source: Interestingly, several crosslinks between the N-terminal region of Chd1 and the DBD are also identified (Figure 3A), suggesting these two regions are close to one another in the intact protein.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from crosslinking data.

claims.claim: The isolated recombinant DBD is able to form an intermolecular complex with a truncated form of Chd1 (residues 1–1010) lacking the DBD.
claims.source: We observe that the isolated recombinant DBD is still able to form an intermolecular complex with a truncated form of Chd1 (residues 1–1010) lacking the DBD (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a result from gel-filtration experiments.

claims.claim: When the N-terminal 133 amino acids are removed from Chd1, the complex with the DBD is no longer formed.
claims.source: Furthermore, when the N-terminal 133 amino acids are removed from Chd1 this complex with the DBD is no longer formed (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is a result from gel-filtration experiments with a deletion mutant.

claims.claim: Contacts between the N-terminus of Chd1 directly contribute to the association with the DBD.
claims.source: This suggests that contacts between the N-terminus of Chd1 directly contribute to the association with the DBD.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the gel-filtration data with deletion mutants.

claims.claim: There is considerable conservation within the 133 amino acids N-terminal to the chromodomains across different yeast species.
claims.source: There is considerable conservation within the 133 amino acids N-terminal to the chromodomains and this includes a tract of acidic amino acids (57-88) followed by a positively charged region extending from 90 to 120.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from sequence alignment analysis.

claims.claim: The N-terminal region of Chd1 includes a tract of acidic amino acids (57-88) followed by a positively charged region extending from 90 to 120.
claims.source: There is considerable conservation within the 133 amino acids N-terminal to the chromodomains and this includes a tract of acidic amino acids (57-88) followed by a positively charged region extending from 90 to 120.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from sequence analysis.

claims.claim: Deletion of residues 57–88 results in loss of interaction with the DBD.
claims.source: Indeed, when we delete just residues 57–88 the interaction with the DBD is also lost (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is a result from gel-filtration experiments with a deletion mutant.

claims.claim: The acidic patch (residues 57-88) plays an important role in mediating interactions with the DBD.
claims.source: Thus, this acidic patch appears to play an important role in mediating interactions with the DBD.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the deletion mutant data.

claims.claim: Deletion of the acidic patch (△57–88) increased nucleosome sliding activity 2-fold.
claims.source: Deletion of the acidic patch was observed to increase nucleosome sliding 2-fold, while deletion of the basic region shows no sliding activity (Figure 4B,C).
claims.evidence: This is a result from nucleosome repositioning assays.

claims.claim: Deletion of the basic region (△90-120) shows no sliding activity.
claims.source: Deletion of the acidic patch was observed to increase nucleosome sliding 2-fold, while deletion of the basic region shows no sliding activity (Figure 4B,C).
claims.evidence: This is a result from nucleosome repositioning assays.

claims.claim: Deletion of the entire N-terminal 133 amino acids increased activity 1.5-fold.
claims.source: Deletion of the entire N-terminal 133 amino acids increased activity 1.5-fold (data not shown), while deletion of the extreme N-terminal 35 residues reduced activity 20-fold (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is a result from nucleosome repositioning assays.

claims.claim: Deletion of the extreme N-terminal 35 residues reduced activity 20-fold.
claims.source: Deletion of the entire N-terminal 133 amino acids increased activity 1.5-fold (data not shown), while deletion of the extreme N-terminal 35 residues reduced activity 20-fold (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is a result from nucleosome repositioning assays.

claims.claim: Triple mutation of three conserved lysine residues within the basic region resulted in a greater than 10-fold reduction in activity.
claims.source: Triple mutation of three conserved lysine residues within the basic region resulted in a greater than 10-fold reduction in activity (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is a result from nucleosome repositioning assays.

claims.claim: N-terminal mutants affected ATPase activity, with reduced or increased activity generally correlating with nucleosome sliding activity.
claims.source: These mutants also affected ATPase activity, with reduced or increased activity generally correlating with nucleosome sliding activity (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is a result from ATP hydrolysis assays.

claims.claim: The increased activity of Chd1 △ 57–88 arose primarily from an increased Kcat.
claims.source: The increased activity of Chd1 △ 57–88 arose primarily from an increased Kcat (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is a result from kinetic analysis of ATP hydrolysis.

claims.claim: Chd1 △ 57–88 formed complexes with nucleosomes in the apo state more effectively than wild-type as detected in gel shift assays.
claims.source: In addition, this mutant formed complexes with nucleosomes in the apo state more effectively as detected in gel shift assays (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is a result from nucleosome binding assays.

claims.claim: The Chd1 △ 90–120, △ 1–35 and R20-21A mutations that strongly reduced activity also bound nucleosomes weakly.
claims.source: The Chd1 △ 90–120, △ 1–35 and R20-21A mutations that strongly reduced activity also bound nucleosomes weakly (Figure 4D), while deletion of residues 1–35 enhanced nucleosome binding but was deleterious to enzymatic activity.
claims.evidence: This is a result from nucleosome binding assays.

claims.claim: A more flexible linkage between the ATPase and DBD facilitates productive engagement with nucleosomes.
claims.source: As both the Chd1 △ 57–88 and △ 1–133 deletions that increase activity reduce association between the ATPase and DBD (Figure 3), we speculate that a more flexible linkage facilitates productive engagement with nucleosomes while inactivating mutations may orient these domains less favourably for full activity.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the correlation between activity and domain interactions.

claims.claim: Full length Chd1 or Chd1 △ 57–88 were integrated into the CHD1 locus of an isw1△chd1△ mutant strain for in vivo analysis.
claims.source: To investigate the consequences of this change in activity in vivo, full length Chd1 or Chd1 △ 57–88 were integrated into the CHD1 locus of an isw1△chd1△ mutant strain.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental approach for in vivo studies.

claims.claim: In an isw1△chd1△ mutant strain, positioning of coding region nucleosomes is severely compromised and is partially restored when full length CHD1 is reintegrated.
claims.source: In this strain, positioning of coding region nucleosomes is severely compromised and is partially restored when full length CHD1 is reintegrated (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is a result from MNase-Seq analysis.

claims.claim: When chd1 △ 57–88 is reintegrated, a nucleosomal oscillation is restored with slightly greater amplitude than the wild type.
claims.source: When chd1 △ 57–88 is reintegrated, a nucleosomal oscillation is restored with slightly greater amplitude than the wild type.
claims.evidence: This is a result from MNase-Seq analysis.

claims.claim: The maximal density of nucleosome dyads is offset downstream by four base pairs at nucleosome +3 in the chd1 △ 57–88 strain.
claims.source: In addition, the maximal density of nucleosome dyads is offset downstream by four base pairs at nucleosome +3 and increments of approximately four base pairs at subsequent downstream nucleosomes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a result from MNase-Seq analysis.

claims.claim: The offset in nucleosome positioning in chd1 △ 57–88 is consistent with increased spacing between coding region nucleosomes with alignment to the transcriptional start site retained.
claims.source: This is consistent with increased spacing between coding region nucleosomes with alignment to the transcriptional start site (TSS) retained.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the MNase-Seq data.

claims.claim: Introduction of full length Chd1 on a higher copy number plasmid resulted in a > 3-fold increase in expression.
claims.source: To test whether the total amount of Chd1 activity affected inter-nucleosome spacing full length Chd1 was introduced on a higher copy number plasmid, resulting in a > 3 – fold increase in expression as assessed by Western blotting (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is a result from Western blotting.

claims.claim: Overexpression of full length Chd1 caused a slightly greater increase in nucleosome spacing, approximately six base pairs.
claims.source: The alignment of nucleosomal reads to the genome from this strain indicates a slightly greater increase in nucleosome spacing, approximately six base pairs (Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This is a result from MNase-Seq analysis.

claims.claim: Introduction of chd1 △ 57–88 on the high copy pRS423 plasmid caused a further increase in spacing to approximately 26 base pairs.
claims.source: Introduction of chd1 △ 57–88 on the high copy pRS423 plasmid caused a further increase in spacing to approximately 26 base pairs (Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 3).
claims.evidence: This is a result from MNase-Seq analysis.

claims.claim: Coding region internucleosome spacing is influenced by the level of Chd1 activity present.
claims.source: These observations are consistent with coding region internucleosome spacing being influenced by the level of Chd1 activity present.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the in vivo nucleosome spacing data.

claims.claim: Chd1 can establish arrays of nucleosomes with a range of linker lengths in vivo.
claims.source: They also show that Chd1 can establish arrays of nucleosomes with a range of linker lengths in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the in vivo nucleosome spacing data.

claims.claim: Variable nucleosome spacing may result from competition between different enzymes involved in establishing nucleosome phasing in vivo.
claims.source: It may result from competition between different enzymes involved in establishing nucleosome phasing in vivo (Ocampo et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of variable nucleosome spacing.

claims.claim: Variable nucleosome spacing may result from changes in nucleosome density following alteration of Chd1 activity in chromatin assembly.
claims.source: From changes in nucleosome density following alteration of Chd1 activity in chromatin assembly (Lusser et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of variable nucleosome spacing.

claims.claim: Variable nucleosome spacing may result because increased nucleosome phasing activity drives nucleosomes apart via a statistically driven process.
claims.source: Or simply because increased nucleosome phasing activity drives nucleosomes apart via a statistically driven process (Mavrich et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of variable nucleosome spacing.

claims.claim: Complexes between Chd1 1–1305 and nucleosomes with symmetrical 25 bp linkers were studied by cryo-EM in the apo state.
claims.source: We next sought to study the interaction of Chd1 when engaged with nucleosomes. Cryo-EM was adopted to achieve this and we initially studied the interaction of Chd1 1–1305 with nucleosomes with symmetrical 25 bp linkers using this approach.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental approach for cryo-EM studies.

claims.claim: A volume was obtained for the Chd1-nucleosome apo complex with a resolution of approximately 20 Å.
claims.source: Following 3D classification and refinement, a volume was obtained with a resolution of approximately 20 Å (Figure 6C,D).
claims.evidence: This is a result from cryo-EM analysis.

claims.claim: The in solution model for Chd1 and a mononucleosome could be fitted into the cryo-EM volume of the apo complex.
claims.source: This volume is made up of separate areas into which our in solution model for Chd1 and a mononucleosome could be fitted (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This describes the fitting of models into the cryo-EM volume.

claims.claim: The engagement surface between Chd1 and the mononucleosome in the apo state is minimal.
claims.source: A notable feature of this fit is that the engagement surface between Chd1 and the mononucleosome is minimal.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claims.claim: In the apo state, Chd1 is bound through interactions between the DBD and the ATPase domains are not engaged.
claims.source: The simplest explanation for this mode of engagement would be that Chd1 is bound through interactions between the DBD and the ATPase domains are not engaged.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the cryo-EM structure.

claims.claim: Hyperactive mutants of Chd1, △ 57–88 and △ 1–133, formed complexes with nucleosomes that migrated slightly faster on native gels.
claims.source: We noticed that the hyperactive mutants of Chd1, △ 57–88 and△ 1–133, formed complexes with nucleosomes that migrated slightly faster on native gels (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from native gel electrophoresis.

claims.claim: The faster migration of hyperactive mutant-nucleosome complexes on native gels suggests a more compact structure.
claims.source: This suggests a more compact structure.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the gel mobility data.

claims.claim: Complexes between Chd1 △ 57–88 and nucleosomes bearing an 11 bp asymmetric linker were assembled in the presence of ADP-BeFx for cryo-EM analysis.
claims.source: To characterise this further, complexes between Chd1 △ 57–88 and nucleosomes bearing an 11 bp asymmetric linker were assembled. This linker was selected to reduce the number of different conformations via which Chd1 could potentially interact via it's DBD. These complexes were formed in the presence of the non-hydrolysable ATP analogue ADP-BeFx which has been observed to stimulate binding of other enzymes to nucleosomes (Leonard and Narlikar, 2015; Racki et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental approach for cryo-EM studies of the engaged complex.

claims.claim: 2450 movies were collected for the Chd1 △ 57–88-nucleosome complex and from these 280,000 particles were picked.
claims.source: 2450 movies were collected and from these 280,000 particles picked.
claims.evidence: This describes the data collection for cryo-EM.

claims.claim: 197,602 particles could be assigned into 2D classes consistent with a nucleosome with a bound attachment.
claims.source: 197,602 of these could be assigned into 2D classes that were consistent with a nucleosome with a bound attachment (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the image processing for cryo-EM.

claims.claim: The final volume for the Chd1 △ 57–88-nucleosome complex has a resolution of 15 Å.
claims.source: Solvent masking was applied prior to the final refinement which resulted in a final volume with a resolution of 15 Å (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a result from cryo-EM analysis.

claims.claim: A nucleosome can be docked within the cryo-EM volume of the engaged complex.
claims.source: A nucleosome can be docked within the volume and the DNA volume on the side of the nucleosome lacking linker provides a strong reference point to orient the nucleosome (Figure 7; Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This describes the fitting of structures into the cryo-EM volume.

claims.claim: The position of the chromoATPase is unambiguous in the cryo-EM volume of the engaged complex.
claims.source: The position of the chromoATPase is also unambiguous and the protrusion formed by ATPase lobe 2 and the chromodomains allows the domains to be oriented (Figure 7; Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This describes the fitting of structures into the cryo-EM volume.

claims.claim: Solvent masking was required to reveal the trajectory of the linker DNA in the cryo-EM volume.
claims.source: While the volume occupied by the DBD must be in the general vicinity of the 11 bp linker, solvent masking was required to reveal the trajectory of the linker DNA.
claims.evidence: This describes the image processing approach.

claims.claim: There is a major change in the orientation of the DBD with respect to ATPase lobe 1 between the solution structure and the nucleosome engaged structure.
claims.source: When the alignment of Chd1 DBD and ATPase domain is compared between the solution structure determined by PELDOR and SAXS (Figures 1 and 2) to that in the nucleosome engaged structure (Figure 7), it is clear that a major change in the orientation of the DBD with respect to ATPase lobe 1 takes place (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of structural models.

claims.claim: Docking Chd1 in the solution conformation onto a nucleosome using the location of the chromoATPase domains in the engaged state as a reference point results in steric clashes with the histone octamer.
claims.source: If Chd1 in the conformation observed in solution is docked onto a nucleosome using the location of the chromoATPase domains in the engaged state as a reference point, steric clashes with the histone octamer indicate this is not possible (Figure 7—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This is a result from structural modeling.

claims.claim: The nucleosomal DNA adjacent to the linker is unravelled from the octamer surface in the engaged complex.
claims.source: A prominent feature of the structural model is that the nucleosomal DNA adjacent to the linker is unravelled from the octamer surface.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claims.claim: When intact nucleosomal DNA is modelled into the cryo-EM volume it protrudes into a region of missing density.
claims.source: This is evident as when intact nucleosomal DNA is modelled into the volume it protrudes into a region of missing density (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from modeling into the cryo-EM volume.

claims.claim: Fluorescent dyes were introduced to DNA derived from the 601 nucleosome positioning sequence at specific positions for FRET measurements.
claims.source: Fluorescent dyes were introduced to DNA derived from the 601 nucleosome positioning sequence on either the forward (F) or reverse (R) strand at the indicated positions relative to the nucleosomal dyad axis of symmetry (Figure 8A; Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental approach for FRET measurements.

claims.claim: When Chd1 1–1305 was added to nucleosomes labeled at F−71 and F + 14, no change in FRET efficiency was observed.
claims.source: When Chd1 1–1305 was added to these nucleosomes, no change in FRET efficiency was observed (Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: This is a result from FRET measurements.

claims.claim: The lack of FRET change at F−71 and F + 14 is consistent with the six base pair linker being too short to direct binding of the Chd1 DBD on this side of the nucleosome.
claims.source: This is consistent with the six base pair linker being too short to direct binding of the Chd1 DBD on this side of the nucleosome.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the FRET data.

claims.claim: Binding of Chd1 1–1305 in presence of AMP-PNP caused a reduction in the mean FRET efficiency from 0.5 to 0.3 for nucleosomes labeled at F + 2 and R-66.

results.result: The solution structure of Chd1 was determined using SAXS and PELDOR measurements. SAXS data showed Chd1 is monomeric in solution with the DBD and N-terminal residues contributing to a protrusion adjacent to the ATPase domains. PELDOR distance measurements between 16 site pairs, combined with two independent modeling approaches (Xplor-NIH and TagDock), yielded consistent models (RMSD 2.4 Å) showing the relative orientation of the DBD and chromoATPase domains. The PELDOR-derived model is compatible with SAXS envelopes, and addition of missing loops improved the fit from χ²=11.5 to χ²=2.08.
results.evaluation: The claims are well-supported by complementary biophysical data. Multiple SAXS fragments were analyzed (C28-C34), PELDOR measurements were validated against known crystal structures (C37-C38), and two independent modeling approaches yielded consistent results (C47-C49). The improved fit after adding missing loops (C54) demonstrates internal consistency. The cys-free mutant retained activity (C35), validating the approach.

results.result: The N-terminal region of Chd1 mediates interactions with the DNA-binding domain (DBD). Chemical crosslinking mass spectrometry identified crosslinks between the N-terminus and DBD (C55). Gel-filtration experiments showed that the isolated DBD forms an intermolecular complex with Chd1 1-1010 lacking the DBD (C57), but this interaction is lost when the N-terminal 133 amino acids are deleted (C58) or when just the acidic patch (residues 57-88) is deleted (C62). Sequence analysis revealed conservation of an acidic tract (57-88) followed by a basic region (90-120) in the N-terminus (C60-C61).
results.evaluation: The claims are supported by multiple lines of evidence including crosslinking-MS (C55), gel-filtration with deletion mutants (C57-C58, C62), and sequence conservation analysis (C60-C61). The systematic deletion approach clearly identifies the acidic patch as critical for DBD interaction. The data are internally consistent and use appropriate biochemical methods.

results.result: Mutations in the N-terminus have both positive and negative effects on Chd1 activity. Deletion of the acidic patch (Δ57-88) increased nucleosome sliding 2-fold (C64) and ATPase activity (C69-C70), primarily through increased Kcat, and enhanced nucleosome binding (C71). In contrast, deletion of the basic region (Δ90-120) abolished sliding activity (C65), and deletion of residues 1-35 reduced activity 20-fold (C67). Triple mutation of conserved lysines in the basic region reduced activity >10-fold (C68). Mutations that increased activity (Δ57-88, Δ1-133) reduced association between the ATPase and DBD domains (C73).
results.evaluation: The claims are supported by systematic mutagenesis with multiple functional assays (nucleosome repositioning, ATPase activity, nucleosome binding). The data show clear structure-function relationships with quantitative measurements. The correlation between reduced domain association and increased activity (C73) provides mechanistic insight, though this remains somewhat speculative. The kinetic analysis (C70) strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: The hyperactive Chd1 Δ57-88 mutant affects nucleosome spacing in vivo. In an isw1Δchd1Δ strain, nucleosome positioning is severely compromised and partially restored by reintegrating wild-type CHD1 (C75). The Δ57-88 mutant restored nucleosomal oscillation with slightly greater amplitude than wild-type (C76) and caused a 4 bp downstream offset at nucleosome +3 that incremented at subsequent nucleosomes (C77), consistent with increased inter-nucleosome spacing (C78). Overexpression of wild-type Chd1 (>3-fold) caused ~6 bp increased spacing (C79-C80), while overexpression of Δ57-88 caused ~26 bp increased spacing (C81), indicating that nucleosome spacing is influenced by Chd1 activity levels (C82-C83).
results.evaluation: The claims are supported by genome-wide MNase-Seq data with appropriate controls and quantification. The dose-dependent effect of Chd1 levels on nucleosome spacing (C79-C82) strengthens the conclusion. Western blotting confirmed protein levels (C79). The data demonstrate physiological relevance of the in vitro findings. Triplicate biological replicates were performed.

results.result: Cryo-EM structure of the apo Chd1-nucleosome complex reveals minimal engagement. Chd1 1-1305 was studied with nucleosomes bearing symmetrical 25 bp linkers in the absence of ATP analogs (C87). 3D classification and refinement yielded a volume at ~20 Å resolution (C88) into which the solution model of Chd1 and a mononucleosome could be fitted (C89). A notable feature is that the engagement surface between Chd1 and the nucleosome is minimal (C90), suggesting Chd1 is bound through the DBD while the ATPase domains are not engaged (C91).
results.evaluation: The claims are supported by cryo-EM data with appropriate image processing. The resolution (~20 Å) is modest but sufficient for domain-level interpretation. The minimal engagement surface (C90) is a direct observation from the structure. The interpretation that the DBD is bound while ATPase domains are not engaged (C91) is reasonable given the structural data, though it remains an inference. The structure is consistent with the solution studies.

results.result: Cryo-EM structure of the engaged Chd1-nucleosome complex reveals DNA unwrapping and domain reorientation. The hyperactive Chd1 Δ57-88 mutant was studied with nucleosomes bearing an 11 bp asymmetric linker in the presence of ADP-BeFx (C94). From 2450 movies and 280,000 particles (C95), 197,602 particles were classified (C96) yielding a final volume at 15 Å resolution (C97). The nucleosome and chromoATPase domains could be unambiguously positioned (C98-C99), with solvent masking revealing linker DNA trajectory (C100). Comparison with the solution structure shows a major change in DBD orientation relative to ATPase lobe 1 (C101), with the solution conformation incompatible with nucleosome binding due to steric clashes (C102). The nucleosomal DNA adjacent to the linker is unraveled from the octamer surface (C103-C104).
results.evaluation: The claims are supported by high-quality cryo-EM data with extensive image processing (multiple rounds of 3D classification, particle movie correction, solvent masking). The 15 Å resolution is appropriate for the conclusions drawn. The DNA unwrapping (C103-C104) is directly observed in the structure. The conformational change (C101) is supported by comparison with the solution structure. The steric clash analysis (C102) validates the conformational change. The use of the hyperactive mutant and ADP-BeFx to stabilize the engaged state is well-justified.

results.result: FRET measurements confirm ATP-dependent DNA unwrapping. Fluorescent dyes were introduced at specific positions on nucleosomal DNA (C105). No FRET change was observed at F-71/F+14 with Chd1 1-1305 (C106), consistent with the 6 bp linker being too short for DBD binding on that side (C107). However, at F+2/R-66, Chd1 1-1305 with AMP-PNP reduced mean FRET efficiency from 0.5 to 0.3 (C108), consistent with DNA dissociation 9 bp from the nucleosome edge (C109). The Δ57-88 mutant showed similar FRET changes with both AMP-PNP and ADP-BeFx (C110). DNA dissociation did not extend deep into the nucleosome (R-60 unaffected, C111), but a larger FRET change was observed at R-85 (C112-C113). Kinetic analysis showed that AMP-PNP favored the unwrapped state through both increased unwrapping rate and decreased re-association rate (C114), confirming that DNA unwrapping occurs with wild-type Chd1 (C115) and is favored in the nucleotide-bound state (C116).
results.evaluation: The claims are supported by systematic single-molecule FRET measurements at multiple positions with appropriate controls. The data are consistent with the cryo-EM structure showing DNA unwrapping. The kinetic analysis (C114) provides mechanistic insight into the nucleotide-dependent conformational change. The use of multiple nucleotide analogs (AMP-PNP, ADP-BeFx) and both wild-type and mutant Chd1 strengthens the conclusions. The FRET data provide orthogonal validation of the structural findings.

results.result: Chd1 exists in an auto-inhibited state in solution that must be relieved for nucleosome engagement. The unfavorable alignment of the C-terminal DBD in solution contributes to an auto-inhibited state (C8). The predominant conformation in solution is not capable of binding nucleosomes in the fully engaged active conformation (C153), thus the apo protein is auto-inhibited (C154). Consistent with this, mutations that increase activity (including Δ57-88) have been reported in Chd1 and other remodeling ATPases (C155). Mutations to the N-terminus that increase activity reduce interactions between the DBD and chromoATPase (C156), suggesting that increased flexibility in domain orientation increases the opportunity for productive nucleosome engagement (C157). Regulation of accessory domain orientation represents a potent means of regulating remodeling ATPase activity (C158).
results.evaluation: The claims are supported by the structural data showing incompatibility between the solution and engaged conformations (C153, C102), the mutagenesis data showing that disrupting domain interactions increases activity (C156, C64-C73), and the observation that the solution conformation cannot bind nucleosomes in the engaged state. The auto-inhibition model (C8, C154) is a reasonable interpretation of the data. The broader conclusion about regulation (C158) is well-supported by the data and consistent with findings in related enzymes (C155).

results.result: Chd1 engages nucleosomes in distinct conformations depending on nucleotide state. In the apo state, the DNA-binding domain contacts the edge of the nucleosome (C2). In the presence of ADP-beryllium fluoride, there are additional interactions between the ATPase domain and the adjacent DNA gyre 1.5 helical turns from the dyad axis (C3). Binding in the engaged conformation involves unraveling the outer turn of nucleosomal DNA (C4) and requires substantial reorientation of the DNA-binding domain with respect to the ATPase domains (C5). The orientation of the DNA-binding domain is mediated by sequences in the N-terminus (C6), and mutations to this region have positive and negative effects on Chd1 activity (C7).
results.evaluation: These claims summarize the major findings of the manuscript and are supported by the structural (cryo-EM, SAXS, PELDOR), biochemical (mutagenesis, activity assays), and biophysical (FRET) data described in the other results. The claims accurately reflect the experimental findings and are stated at an appropriate level of confidence.

results.result: Chd1 can engage with nucleosomes in multiple conformations beyond those characterized. The study demonstrates that Chd1 engages nucleosomes in different modes (C118), but additional conformations likely exist with different linker lengths and ATP hydrolysis states (C119). Complexes with two Chd1 molecules per nucleosome can form but were not characterized (C120). Ensemble approaches may report on mixtures of different states (C121).
results.evaluation: These claims appropriately acknowledge the limitations of the study. The observation of multiple binding modes (C118) is directly supported by the apo and engaged structures. The speculation about additional conformations (C119) is reasonable given the complexity of the system. The statement about 2:1 complexes (C120) is supported by gel shift data showing super-shifted bands. The caveat about ensemble methods (C121) is a valid interpretation.

results.result: The DBD binds the first ~10 bp of linker DNA, and this interaction is functionally important. In the engaged complex, the DBD is bound close to the nucleosome edge interacting with the first 10 bp of linker DNA (C127). Previous studies showed that deleting the SANT-SLIDE domains greatly reduces activity (C128), but fusion to heterologous DNA-binding domains restores activity (C129). Optimal positioning for Chd1-AraC hybrids is +8 bp from the nucleosome boundary (C130), and for Chd1-streptavidin fusions is +11 bp (C131). These observations indicate that interaction with the first turn of DNA outside the nucleosome is functionally important (C132), and nucleosome repositioning is directed towards the bound linker (C133).
results.evaluation: The claims integrate the structural findings (C127) with previous functional studies (C128-C131) to draw a well-supported conclusion about the functional importance of DBD positioning (C132-C133). The structural data are consistent with the optimal positioning determined in previous studies. The interpretation is reasonable and well-supported.

results.result: The chromoATPase domain engages nucleosomal DNA at SHL 1.5, in a distinct arrangement from ISW2. ATP-dependent repositioning occurs through the chromoATPase domain engaging nucleosomal DNA centered 1.5 superhelical turns off the dyad (C138). This SHL 1.5 location is 90 bp from the bound linker on the linear sequence (C139) but in closer spatial proximity once DNA is wrapped (C140). This arrangement differs from ISW2, where the proximal dyad location is bound by the ATPase domains (C141-C142). The distinct topography raises the possibility that DNA translocation orientation differs from other enzymes (C143).
results.evaluation: The claims are supported by the cryo-EM structure showing the position of the chromoATPase domain (C138-C140). The comparison with ISW2 (C141-C142) is based on published crosslinking data and is accurate. The speculation about translocation directionality (C143) is appropriately cautious and acknowledges that the resolution is insufficient to determine strand specificity (C144).

results.result: The cryo-EM structure has limitations but is consistent with recent crosslinking data. The resolution does not enable assignment of strand specificity of nucleic acid contacts (C144) or comment on rearrangements between domains during DNA engagement (C145). However, a recent crosslinking study (C146) identified major DNA contacts by the DBD, chromodomains, and ATPase domain that are consistent with the model (C147). The cryo-EM model is reinforced by orthogonal FRET and crosslinking data (C148).
results.evaluation: These claims appropriately acknowledge the limitations of the structural data (C144-C145) while noting consistency with independent crosslinking data (C146-C147). The statement about orthogonal validation (C148) is well-supported by the FRET data and published crosslinking studies. This demonstrates scientific rigor in acknowledging limitations while highlighting strengths.

results.result: DNA unwrapping may prime the nucleosome for ATP-dependent remodeling. Loss of octamer contacts on the bound side reduces the energy required for dynamic alterations to nucleosomal DNA (C134) and may act as a priming step for subsequent ATP-dependent remodeling (C135). This priming step may distinguish initial ATP-dependent changes from subsequent cycles (C136). Consistent with this, 7 bp of DNA have been observed to be removed from nucleosomes by ISW2 and Isw1b followed by 3 bp movements (C137).
results.evaluation: These claims are speculative (C134-C136) and represent a mechanistic hypothesis rather than a directly demonstrated result. While the DNA unwrapping is clearly observed (C103-C104, C108-C116), the functional significance as a 'priming step' is inferred. The comparison with ISW2/Isw1b (C137) provides some support but does not directly test the priming hypothesis. Additional experiments would be needed to test this model.

results.result: Large-scale nucleotide-dependent conformational changes have been observed in related enzymes. A large-scale conformational change in SNF2h has been reported (C149), involving repositioning of the SANT-SLIDE DBD from +20 bp to -25 bp (C150). This could involve redistribution from positions along the linker to high occupancy at the nucleosome boundary (C151). Evidence for conformational changes upon DNA binding has also been obtained for Drosophila ISWI by protease digestion (C152).
results.evaluation: These claims accurately summarize published findings on related enzymes (C149-C152) and provide context for the Chd1 findings. The citations are appropriate and the interpretations are reasonable. This contextualizes the Chd1 results within the broader field.

results.result: Regulation of remodeling enzyme activity may be important for managing nuclear ATP levels. The combined abundance of chromatin remodeling enzymes could present a load on nuclear ATP levels (C159). Regulation allowing increased activity when chromatin organization is required would reduce energy expenditure (C160).
results.evaluation: These claims are speculative and not directly tested in the manuscript. While the auto-inhibition mechanism is well-supported (C153-C158), the physiological significance in terms of ATP management (C159-C160) is hypothetical. This represents an interesting hypothesis but lacks experimental support.

results.result: Chd1 activity may be influenced by linker length to achieve nucleosome spacing. The activity of Chd1 is anticipated to be influenced by the length of DNA between adjacent nucleosomes (C162). In the ISWI-related ACF complex, pause duration is shortened when linker lengths increase from 40-60 bp (C163), and the AutoN activation mutation impedes DNA length sensing (C164). This may function similarly to the hyperactive Chd1 Δ57-88 mutant (C165). However, there may be important differences between ISWI and Chd1 SANT-SLIDE domains (C166-C167). Yeast Chd1 organizes nucleosomes with relatively short 16 bp linkers (C168), and engagement with the first turn of extranucleosomal DNA provides a means of achieving activity within close-packed arrays (C169). Steric clashes would be anticipated when linker length falls below 20 bp, reducing activity (C170). Inhibition of repositioning at low linker lengths is sufficient to drive even spacing via a bidirectional statistical process (C171).
results.evaluation: These claims are largely speculative and represent a mechanistic model for how Chd1 might sense linker length to achieve nucleosome spacing. While the structural data (C169) and in vivo spacing data (C168, C74-C83) are well-supported, the specific mechanism of linker length sensing (C162, C170) is not directly tested. The comparisons with ACF/ISWI (C163-C167) provide context but do not validate the model for Chd1. The statistical spacing model (C171) is cited but not experimentally tested here.
